title: A Comparison of Responses from Human Therapists and Large Language Model–Based Chatbots to Assess Therapeutic Communication: Mixed Methods Study
population: Licensed therapists with at least 1 year of professional experience evaluating chatbot and therapist responses to scripted fictional mental health scenarios
country_or_setting: United States; Stanford University; therapists recruited via Psychology Today listings, email lists, word of mouth; chatbot interactions evaluated in scripted text-based scenarios
ai_type_application: Large language model–based chatbots; general-purpose AI assistants and AI companions used for mental health conversations
ai_exposure_intervention: Three chatbots (ChatGPT/GPT-4, Pi, Replika) generated responses to two fictional mental health scenarios; therapists reviewed six chatbot interaction logs and compared them with their own responses. Seven chatbots were initially tested overall.
comparator_control_group: Human licensed therapists responding to the same scripted scenarios
mental_health_outcome: Therapeutic communication quality and suitability for mental health support, including handling of depression/social anxiety symptoms, suicidal ideation, empathy/validation, inquiry, advice-giving, and crisis response
outcome_measurement_tool: Multitheoretical List of Therapeutic Interventions (MULTI) coding; therapist rankings; think-aloud procedure; semistructured interviews; thematic analysis; word count comparison
positive_effects: Chatbots displayed elements of good therapy such as validation, normalization, empathy, reflection, reassurance, affirmation, and some psychoeducation. AI companions were sometimes perceived as more conversational and humanlike.
negative_effects_harms: Chatbots overused directive advice and psychoeducation, asked insufficient open-ended questions, provided generic one-size-fits-all suggestions, lacked feedback seeking, were perceived as limited in building therapeutic relationships, and handled crisis situations poorly. Reported risks included failure to perform adequate suicide risk assessment, delayed or absent referral to crisis resources, possible amplification of problematic judgments, potential user attachment/dependence, and possible degradation of social skills with long-term use.
evidence_type: Primary empirical mixed-methods comparative study with quantitative coding and qualitative therapist assessments
main_finding: General-purpose LLM-based chatbots were judged unsuitable to safely engage in mental health conversations, especially in crisis situations. Compared with therapists, chatbots used more affirming, reassuring, psychoeducational, and suggestive language but asked fewer elaborative questions and tended to provide generic, directive advice.
effect_size_key_result: Therapists evoked more elaboration than chatbots (U=9; P=.001; r=-0.65). Chatbots used more suggestions (U=12.5; P=.003; r=-0.61), reassurance (U=23; P=.02; r=-0.47), psychoeducation (U=22.5; P=.02; r=-0.48), and affirmation (U=28; P=.045; r=-0.41). Therapists wrote fewer words overall than chatbots (U=10; P=.002; r=0.64).

controlled_confounders.family_social_factors: Scenario responses were scripted and standardized across therapists and chatbots for direct comparison
controlled_confounders.other_confounders: Therapists were blinded to which chatbot produced each response

limitations_bias: Small sample size (N=17), scripted hypothetical scenarios with limited ecological validity, brief interactions only, no direct assessment of real user mental health outcomes or effectiveness, rapidly changing chatbot models, incomplete coverage of all available chatbots, and findings based on therapist judgments rather than patient outcomes.
relevance_to_our_review: Relevant to AI effects on mental health because it evaluates how widely used LLM chatbots may influence mental health support quality and identifies potential benefits and harms, especially around crisis response and problematic long-term reliance. However, it does not measure actual patient mental health outcomes.
reason_for_decision: Useful for background and harm/safety evidence on AI in mental health support, but not a direct study of mental health effects on end users or clinical outcomes.
notes_for_research_question: This paper is best used for evidence on mechanisms, communication quality, and safety concerns rather than effectiveness. It suggests possible negative downstream effects such as overreliance, attachment, and poor crisis handling, but these were inferred by therapists rather than measured in users.
